Dans le quotidien d’un organisme d’aide: A Day in the Life of an Immigrant Aid Organization

Après de nombreux arrêts, les portes de: After many stops, the elevator doors of this tower on Côte-des-Neiges Road open. The doors of the Service d’Interprète, d’Aide et de Référence aux Immigrants (SIARI) won’t open for a few more minutes, but dozens and dozens of people, most of them asylum seekers, have already formed a long line to get help.
La journée sera donc semblable à celle d: So the day will be much like yesterday, and all those that came before it since the start of the pandemic. For more than 40 years, SIARI has supported and accompanied new immigrants, refugees and their families. Whether through interpretation services for everyday activities, French-language classes or computer support for immigration procedures, SIARI helps newcomers, who often speak neither French nor English, overcome these barriers.
Dans une salle située de l’autre côté de: In a room across the elevator shaft, about ten SIARI employees are having lunch together among the cubicles before going back on duty. The scene is pretty ordinary in itself, and yet it’s the first time in a long while that almost all of them have managed to get together for a break.
Ce rare moment infusé de légèreté, ils l: They owe this rare, lighthearted moment to a board member who stopped by earlier in the morning to talk with them about their working conditions, which have become unbearable.
C’est sur un ton ironique, tout en antic: It is in an ironic tone, already anticipating their answer, that SIARI executive director Fatma Djebbar addresses her employees to gauge the weight of the overwork they endure.
« Qui va aux toilettes deux fois dans un: “Who goes to the bathroom twice in a day?” she asks her employees from the end of the table.
Les rires jaunes non moins dénués de sen: The bitter, knowing laughter that fills the room answers the question indirectly. Unsurprisingly, the reaction is the same when Fatma asks who takes their unpaid one-hour lunch break.
« On a des rendez-vous de planifiés et c: “We have appointments scheduled and it’s already full, but then there are people without appointments on top of that,” explains Sharmila, one of the employees.
Partie entre-temps chercher son agenda,: Having gone off in the meantime to get her planner, Yolanda shows what the coming week looks like for her. Every day is packed with appointments back to back, hour after hour, from morning until evening, and even on the weekend.
« C’est mon agenda sans les rendez-vous: “This is my schedule without the walk-ins; I don’t add the people without appointments, otherwise it’s a lot,” she explains, looking at a planner that would be a source of anxiety for many.
« Il y a quelques années, on pouvait enc: “A few years ago, we could still go out, take a walk, go to someone’s place after work, but now that’s over,” says another employee. “You come home at night to eat, and then you stay on your couch until the next morning. On the weekend, it takes you all of Saturday to recover from the week.”
Assise en bout de table, Fatma Djebbar r: Seated at the end of the table, Fatma Djebbar says gravely that, as proof of her employees’ distress, their group insurance premiums have doubled this year.
Parmi les solutions évoquées plus tôt av: Among the solutions discussed earlier with the board of directors is hiring a social worker, not for the beneficiaries, but for SIARI’s employees.
Aussitôt la pause terminée, tout le mond: As soon as the break is over, everyone heads back to the front lines. The bustle quickly resumes in the maze of hallways where the world’s languages intertwine.
Un employé interpelle son collègue au fo: An employee calls out to a colleague at the far end of a hallway near the printer to ask a favour.
« Tu as vu tout le monde dans mon bureau: “Did you see everyone in my office? It’s going to be very long,” his colleague replies.
Tous les membres de l’équipe sont issus: All the members of the team are immigrants themselves and have therefore experienced firsthand the twists and turns of Canada’s immigration process.
Pour Fatma, il ne fait aucun doute que l: For Fatma, there is no doubt that their life stories make them even more sensitive to the reality of the people they serve.
« Ils ne se rendent même pas compte qu’i: “They don’t even realize they’re changing lives every day,” the director says in front of her employees.
« On change des vies sur un détail, ajou: “We change lives over a detail,” adds Fatma. “When you lose your keys, you go see a locksmith, but there are people who can’t talk to the locksmith to get him to come and change the lock because they speak neither English nor French.”
Cette empathie et ce désir profond d’aid: This empathy and deep desire to help people who speak neither of the two official languages make it even harder for employees to turn down certain requests that asylum seekers see as vital.
« Ils sont pour la plupart conseillers e: “They’re mostly integration advisers, but they become social workers, translators, companions, nurses, doctors, teachers,” Fatma says with dismay. All the employees nod in agreement without hesitation.
Hier encore, une personne parlant unique: Just yesterday, a person who spoke only Ukrainian and didn’t know whom to turn to called SIARI to find a gynecologist.
« On n’est pas financés pour les choses: “We’re not funded for the things they do every day; even for registering asylum seekers on the Ministry of Immigration’s portal, we’re not subsidized for that,” says SIARI’s director. Yet hundreds of people come to the organization to fill out the notorious platform.
Sur son budget annuel d’environ 1,4 M$,: Of its annual budget of about $1.4 million, only $119,000 is granted each year to SIARI’s mission, or 8.5 per cent of its total budget.
« Les gouvernements, autant provinciaux: “The governments, provincial and federal alike, wash their hands of it. They subsidize us with crumbs and wash their hands of their responsibilities,” says Fatma Djebbar. “Right now it’s the community sector that’s supporting communities, and that’s not normal anymore.”
Elle déplore l’absence totale de communi: She laments the total absence of communication between her organization and the federal government.
Les membres de l’équipe profitent ainsi: The team members take the opportunity to list various measures imposed by governments that, in their view, only make their work heavier.
Parmi les récentes mesures se trouve l’o: Among the recent measures is the requirement that asylum seekers register on the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) portal using a computer.
Cette exigence remplit chaque jour la sa: This requirement fills the computer room every day, a room SIARI improvised in a hurry to cope with the massive arrival of asylum seekers without computer equipment. “You can feel that decisions are made in offices, whether at the federal or provincial level,” says Fatma. “They don’t see the impact [of their decisions] on people.”
Une autre mesure qui force de nombreuses: Another measure that forces many people to come to the organization is registration for the Quebec Ministry of Immigration’s French-language classes. Although these classes are meant for people who don’t speak the language of Molière, registration is done… in French. SIARI therefore helps them so they can sign up for the French classes needed to settle in Quebec.
Pour répondre au flux massif de personne: To handle the massive flow of people seeking help, SIARI’s employees have also had to improvise as interior designers.
Depuis le début de la pandémie, une diza: Since the start of the pandemic, about ten desks have had to be added to meet demand. Rooms that used to hold a single desk and a single employee now hold three. The meeting room and even the kitchen have both had to be converted to fit cubicles and desks.
Pour Fatma, le financement à la mission: For Fatma, core mission funding would also allow them to find bigger premises and hire more staff.
Sergine L. a commencé à travailler au SI: Sergine L. began working at SIARI before the pandemic. She has seen how the situation within the organization has evolved.
Sergine L. est chargée de projet pour le: Sergine L. is a project manager for asylum seekers. Like each of her colleagues, she works with her heart, even at a cost to herself. Yet it is with a smile that she confides she doesn’t have “enough hours in a day” to keep up with the workload.
« À partir de 14 h. je suis obligée d’ar: “From 2 p.m. on, I have to stop taking asylum seekers for registration on the IRCC portal, because last time it was almost 6 p.m. and I was still here, when it’s supposed to close at 4 p.m.,” she says. “I had to start doing that, because I also don’t want to exhaust my colleagues.”
Depuis le début de la journée, Sergine a: Since the start of the day, Sergine has seen no fewer than sixty asylum seekers come to SIARI for help for various reasons. “They come every day, but not necessarily for the IRCC portal. They also come for other things, like the housing allowance and baby registration,” she explains.
« Ce matin, on a eu une famille de deman: “This morning, we had a family of asylum seekers where the mother had given birth two months ago but didn’t know how to register her child,” she adds.
Elle dit que le rythme de travail était: She says the pace of work was “rather calm” when she was hired in 2021. Then the reopening of the borders imposed a new rhythm, filling SIARI’s hallways with hundreds of asylum seekers.
« Je sentais que j’allais perdre la tête: “I felt like I was going to lose my mind,” says Sergine. “I even came in secretly on Saturdays to help fill out forms, because I have so much empathy for these people.”
Au moment d’évoquer l’épuisement qu’elle: As she speaks of the exhaustion she feels, Sergine stops smiling, and her eyes well up. She admits that even bringing up the subject can bring tears. “I’m overwhelmed, I don’t have enough time and I’m incapable of saying ‘no,’” she confides. “At the end of the day, it goes very badly, because I’m like a vegetable on my couch.”
Face à la détresse des demandeurs d’asil: Faced with the distress of asylum seekers caught in the complexity of their new host society, Sergine blames herself for not finding the strength to turn down their requests. “Even inside me, when I want to say ‘no,’ I can’t,” she says. “These are people who are vulnerable, after all, but they don’t understand that we at SIARI need to rest in order to function.”
En plus de la fatigue causée par la quan: On top of the fatigue caused by the sheer amount of work, SIARI’s employees must also cope with the life stories of the asylum seekers. These stories are often branded by the horror and persecution they lived through, which forced them to seek asylum in Canada.
Dans leur demande d’asile, les personnes: In their asylum claims, people must demonstrate that they were persecuted in their country of origin. For integration advisers, there is no choice but to listen to these horror stories all day long and then inform claimants about IRCC. But for some employees, these stories take them back to their own past.
C’est le cas de Raquel*, une demandeuse: That is the case for Raquel*, an asylum seeker from Colombia who works at SIARI. Every week, she helps no fewer than thirty Spanish-speaking asylum seekers fill out the Ministry of Immigration’s forms.
« Ils doivent nous raconter tout ce qui: “They have to tell us everything that happened in their country,” she says. “There are people who were raped because they’re part of the LGBTQ+ community, women who were victims of domestic violence, or families who were persecuted because they were in contact with drug traffickers.”
Certains demandeurs hésitent à lui donne: Some claimants hesitate to give her details, but for others, Raquel is the first person in a long time they can confide in. The young woman says there are “no happy stories” in anything she hears.
« C’est dur pour moi, car il y a beaucou: “It’s hard for me, because there are many cases in which I see my own story,” she adds. “You put yourself in people’s shoes and it’s tiring, but we try to do our best.” She herself had to leave her native Colombia with her family because her sister was being persecuted because of her gender identity and sexual orientation. Faced with the horror stories she hears all day long, she admits she sometimes feels she is “sacrificing her mental health.”
« C’est comme si tu revivais la même cho: “It’s as if you’re reliving the same thing, but in other people’s skin,” says Raquel. “This week, I got home and cried in my sister’s arms, because it’s a burden, all these emotions.”
À peine est-elle remise de ses émotions: She has barely recovered from her emotions when a colleague rushes down the hallway to call out to Raquel and two other colleagues. “In five minutes, we’re celebrating Yolanda’s birthday!” he announces, rounding up as many people as possible.
De retour dans la salle où l’équipe dîna: Back in the room where the team had lunch earlier, about twenty employees rush in, along with their director Fatma. Everyone seems to have set the weight of work aside for a few moments to celebrate the birthday of Yolanda, one of SIARI’s longest-serving employees.
Les employés du SIARI se réunissent pour: SIARI employees gather to celebrate their colleague Yolanda’s birthday.
« Une tradition au SIARI, c’est qu’on fê: “A tradition at SIARI is that we celebrate every birthday!” says Fatma after Yolanda, or Yollie as her colleagues like to call her, blows out the candles on the cake bought for the occasion. “Thanks, everyone!” Yolanda replies, delighted by the surprise they prepared for her.
À peine les parts de gâteau sont-elle fi: The cake slices are barely finished when director Fatma calls her troops back to the reality of work: “Everyone, there are a lot of people waiting in the hallway.”
Encore une fois, le moment de répit a ét: Once again, the moment of respite was short-lived.
